# Adequate calculations, models and uncertainty {#sec-model-adequacy}

An engineer can calculate a delay to many digits and still make the wrong receiver
decision. Numerical precision does not identify the physical delay, and a correct
uncertainty formula does not establish its input assumptions. We need a method
for deciding which approximation is adequate, which uncertainty matters, and what
evidence is missing before a result can support a design choice.

[Chapter 5](phase-delay-inference.qmd) supplies the inference example;
[Chapter 2](scalar-stochastic-phase.qmd) supplies scalar stochastic reasoning,
[Chapter 3](observation-weighted-coherence.qmd) supplies the Gaussian moments
and exponential-covariance average used below, and
[Chapter 4](covariance-quadratic-forms.qmd) supplies the covariance bridge. Here we assess a calculation built from those results rather than
create another competing phase or covariance convention. Positive physical delay
still gives negative input-oriented phase slope. Local envelope, phase and
spectral conventions remain local. The examples are synthetic teaching models,
not measurement uncertainty certificates or experimentally validated receivers.

## Start with a decision and its scales

Suppose two input-oriented phase observations at known physical frequencies
f1 and f2 are intended to estimate a total differential delay. Define
Delta_f=f2-f1>0 and dphi=phi2-phi1 on a justified unwrapped branch. A pure-delay
model with constant phase intercept gives

$$
 \tau=-{d\phi\over2\pi\Delta f}.
$$

The phase observations must already be translated through receiver conversion
orientation as explained in Chapter 5. Unknown receiver-path delay remains part
of the total; it does not vanish through this formula. We ask whether the model
can support an illustrative 0.15 ns standard-deviation target. That target is a
precision criterion, not a total-error or accuracy requirement.

Dimensional analysis checks the interface: radians divided by Hz yields seconds,
with the numerical 2 pi converting phase to cycles. Useful dimensionless scales
include phase error relative to one radian, frequency uncertainty relative to
Delta_f, and unmodeled phase curvature relative to fitted phase change. A small
parameter must control the neglected term, not merely be numerically small in
arbitrary units. For delay inference, even tiny voltage noise near an amplitude
null can give large phase error; voltage scale alone is the wrong criterion.

## Derive sensitivity and retain covariance

Let p be a vector of input quantities, p0 its nominal value and delta p a centered
small perturbation with covariance C_p. For the following quadratic-order
remainder, assume h is twice continuously differentiable with bounded second
derivatives throughout the relevant scaled input region. Taylor expansion gives

$$
 h(p_0+\delta p)=h(p_0)+g\,\delta p+O(\|\delta p\|^2),\qquad
 g_i={\partial h\over\partial p_i}\bigg|_{p_0}.
$$

The row g contains sensitivity coefficients. After declaring compatible coordinate
scales, its entries carry output units per input unit. Expanding the variance
of the first-order term yields

$$
 \operatorname{var}h\simeq g C_p g^T
 =\sum_i g_i^2 C_{ii}+2\sum_{i<j}g_i g_j C_{ij}.
$$

This is Chapter 4's quadratic form applied to the linearized output. It is exact
for an affine h, otherwise approximate. The first neglected mean correction is
one half the sum of Hessian entries H_ij=partial²h/(partial p_i partial p_j)
times C_ij, provided the second-order expansion has an integrable remainder
small relative to retained terms over the input distribution. For example, bounded
third derivatives throughout its support and a sufficiently small third absolute
perturbation moment control that remainder. Differentiability alone does not
justify a quadratic remainder: h(x)=|x|^(3/2) at zero has zero derivative but a
remainder larger than order x².
This warns that h(E[p]) need not equal E[h(p)]. Covariance-aware first-order
uncertainty propagation and inclusion of significant measurement-process inputs
are also specified in [NIST TN 1297, Appendix A.1–A.3](https://www.nist.gov/pml/nist-technical-note-1297/nist-tn-1297-appendix-law-propagation-uncertainty).
The theorem does not supply a missing physical input model.

A covariance may describe repeated receiver variability, uncertainty about a
fixed path parameter, or uncertainty of an estimator. These are different
ensembles or states of knowledge. Identify which is intended before combining
them. A confidence or coverage claim also requires distributional assumptions;
standard deviation alone does not specify a tail probability. A full measurement
uncertainty procedure and calibration evidence belong to later metrology work.

## Follow the delay budget through a changed assumption

Assume Delta_f=10 MHz and true total delay 5 ns. Then nominal dphi=-0.314159265 rad.
Let the centered phase errors be delta_phi1=u+e1 and delta_phi2=u+e2. The common
source u here is a frequency-independent phase-offset component common to
simultaneous multitone comparisons with identical normalized time weighting in
one fixed acquisition state. It is the same random draw in both observations,
not a universal oscillator timing-error model. Its variance is 0.00036 rad²; independent local terms e1,e2 each have variance
0.00004 rad² and are independent of u. Thus individual phase variances are
0.0004 rad², covariance is 0.00036 rad², and difference variance is 0.00008 rad².
This is a declared source/path construction, not a chosen correlation coefficient.

The phase sensitivities of tau are +1/(2 pi Delta_f) and -1/(2 pi Delta_f), so
the predicted delay standard deviation is

$$
 u_\tau={\sqrt{0.00008}\over2\pi\,10^7}\ {\rm s}
 =0.142353\ {\rm ns}.
$$

The illustrative precision target is met under the stated model. Incorrectly
treating the two phase errors as independent gives 0.450158 ns and would reject
the same design for the wrong reason. Conversely, deleting local noise because
the source is shared would be unjustified. Shared contributions cancel only
because their phase sensitivities and observation timing match in this model.
For sequential or differently filtered observations, replace u by distinct shared
source draws with equal variance V=0.00036 and correlation rho. Difference variance
then becomes 0.00008+2V(1-rho). The 0.15 ns target requires rho at least about
0.987741. This rho describes the shared-source draws, not the total phase errors.
Chapter 3 supplies the observation-dependent covariance calculation needed before
reusing that cancellation assumption.

For a concrete local input model, let Delta_f uncertainty be uniform on
[-sqrt(3)1000,+sqrt(3)1000] Hz about its 10 MHz nominal value, independent of
the phase inputs. Its standard uncertainty is 1000 Hz and its support stays far
from zero. Then its sensitivity is -tau/Delta_f. Its first-order contribution is
0.0005 ns standard uncertainty at the nominal point, negligible beside the phase
term here. That is a model-specific comparison. A frequency-scale bias or a
correlated phase/frequency error needs its own term and cannot be hidden inside
an independent variance. The reciprocal-frequency Taylor expansion is local. A small relative standard
uncertainty alone does not control rare near-zero gaps, where reciprocal moments
can become enormous or fail to exist. Justify support away from zero or adequate
tail/remainder control before treating the linearized variance as an adequate
output-uncertainty model; the bounded uniform model supplies that condition here.

Now change only the shared-source path: give channel 2 sensitivity 0.5 to u.
Difference variance becomes 0.25(0.00036)+0.00008=0.00017 rad², giving about
0.20751 ns standard deviation. The precision decision reverses. Neither more
digits in the solver nor a positive covariance matrix can rescue the original
conclusion after this physical assumption changes.

## A zero derivative does not mean zero uncertainty

Consider a normalized quadrature observation y=sin(phi) near phi=pi/2. Write
phi=pi/2+delta with delta centered Gaussian of variance sigma²; then y=cos(delta).
The derivative with respect to delta at zero vanishes, so first-order propagation
predicts zero variance. The prediction is inadequate, not evidence of a noiseless
observation. The expansion y≈1-delta²/2 instead gives a mean shift -sigma²/2
and variance sigma^4/2, using the Gaussian fourth moment developed in Chapter 3.

There is an independent exact check. Chapter 3's Gaussian characteristic function
gives E[cos(delta)]=exp(-sigma²/2). The identity cos²(delta)=(1+cos(2delta))/2
then gives

$$
 E[y]=e^{-\sigma^2/2},\qquad
 \operatorname{var}y={1\over2}(1-e^{-\sigma^2})^2.
$$

At sigma=0.2 rad, the exact mean is 0.980199 and standard deviation is 0.0277261;
the second-order approximation gives 0.0282843. An illustrative y-standard-deviation
limit of 0.01 fails despite the first-order zero. Moreover y cannot distinguish
+delta from -delta. Inverting near this maximum introduces branch ambiguity and
large sensitivity; a small output change cannot be interpreted as a unique phase
change. Nonlinear propagation, a distribution or interval calculation, and the
actual identifiable observable must replace an invalid first-order result.

## Numerical agreement must be about distinct formulations

The finite-average variance for exponential phase covariance in Chapter 3 contains
the dimensionless factor

$$
 g(x)={2(x-1+e^{-x})\over x^2},\qquad x=T/t_c>0.
$$

This is a numerical evaluation example of that existing result, not a new canonical
derivation. Its physical limit as x tends to zero is one: the phase is nearly
constant within a short observation. Direct floating-point subtraction at x=1e-8
can produce g≈2.220446 on the tested Python environment. It subtracts nearly equal
numbers and then divides the rounding error by x². More printed digits do not help.

Expand exp(-x) before subtracting: g=1-x/3+x²/12-x³/60+..., giving approximately
0.999999996667 at that x. A distinct time-domain check is
2 integral_0^1 (1-v)exp(-xv) dv. It avoids the cancellation and can be quadratured
with resolution refinement. A converged integral and a stable series test numerical
consistency; they do not prove that an actual receiver has exponential covariance.

Specify numerical error relative to the decision margin. Refine integration step
or spectral cutoff, inspect changes and bound a neglected tail where possible.
Step refinement alone can miss oscillatory structure if both grids undersample it;
a shared formula in two programs can preserve the same sign error. Compare a
different formulation, asymmetry, units and limits before interpreting agreement.
For the inference and tracking examples, use source sums versus covariance, time
integration versus transfer response, and known ambiguity cases as separate checks.

## Choose the smallest model that preserves the decision

Separate four questions in the report: encoded mathematical correctness, numerical
error, input uncertainty and model discrepancy. Model discrepancy is the difference
between the chosen physical representation and the relevant actual behavior at
specified inputs and states. It is not automatically an independent random noise
term. Without physical evidence its magnitude may remain unknown.

A pure-delay model may be enough for an introductory local fit. Frequency-dependent
path response, asynchronous sampling or drift during a sweep may require a richer
model. An unmodeled 0.5 ns receiver path would bias a DUT-referred result by 0.5 ns
while preserving a perfectly linear phase slope. Passing the 0.15 ns precision
target does not bound that bias. Calibration or independent path evidence is needed
before claiming DUT accuracy. Computational refinement cannot provide it.

For a transfer assessment, halve Delta_f without changing the declared phase
covariance: delay standard deviation doubles, reversing the nominal precision
decision. Then retain Delta_f but change the common-source coupling as above;
reconstruct C_p before propagating it. Finally compare a desired slow phase
variation in a tracking residual with the same variation in the correction output
in [Chapter 7](tracking-signal-retention.qmd). A quieter output can represent
signal suppression rather than a more accurate physical model. Adequacy is judged
against the observable and decision, with unsupported extrapolations left explicit.
